content: First flash your devices with our binary from [Releases tab](https://github.com/openshwprojects/OpenBK7231T_App/releases), then follow steps from [FLASHING.md](https://github.com/openshwprojects/OpenBK7231T_App/blob/main/FLASHING.md) or watch our [flashing tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L6d42IMGhHw). An open access point should appear after flashing. Connect to it, open page at 192.168.4.1 (or on BL602 it may be 192.168.169.1), go to Config->WiFi, enter your WiFi SSID/pass, reboot, and finally check your DHCP page for new device IP. You can use MAC reservation to keep constant IP. Next you need to setup the pins of the device (GPIO roles), you can figure them out yourself, use a [device template](https://openbekeniot.github.io/webapp/devicesList.html) (device template can be applied in Web Application, click Open Web Application button), or [ask on our forum](https://www.elektroda.com/rtvforum/forum390.html). Then you can configure your MQTT, use HASS Discovery, etc.

shortDesc: a method to recover device from wrong SSID/pass or crashing config
content: Device is counting full boots (full boot is a boot after which device worked for 30 seconds). If you power off and on device multiple times, it will enter open access point mode and safe mode (safe mode means even pin systems are not initialized). Those modes are used to recover devices from bad configs and errors.

topic: Simple TCP command server for scripting
shortDesc: a simple TCP interface for scripting
content:
You can enable a simple TCP server in device Generic/Flags option, which will listen by default on port 100. Server can accept single connection at time from PuTTY in RAW mode (raw TCP connection) and accepts text commands for OpenBeken console. In future, we may add support for multiple connections at time. Server will close connection if client does nothing for some time.

  There are some extra short commands for TCP console:
- GetChannel [index] 
- GetReadings - returns voltage, current and power
- ShortName 
the commands above return a single ASCII string as a reply so it's easy to parse.

shortDesc: an easy HA pairing method with [Discovery](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pkcspey25V4) or Yaml gen
content:
MQTT based integration with Home Assistant is possible in 2 ways from the Home Assistant configuration page (`Config > Generate Home Assistant cfg`).

 You can paste the generated [yaml](https://www.home-assistant.io/docs/configuration/yaml/) configuration into Home Assistant configuration manually. You can also improve this YAML, edit it however you like, because for some advanced devices the autogenerated config might be empty

Or add the devices automatically via discovery (see [YT tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pkcspey25V4). To do click the `Start Home Assistant Discovery` button which sends outs [MQTT discovery](https://www.home-assistant.io/docs/mqtt/discovery/) messages, one for each entity (switch, light).
* The discovery topic should match the `discovery_prefix` defined in Home Assistant, the default value is `homeassistant`.
* More details about Home Assistant discovery can be found [here](https://www.home-assistant.io/docs/mqtt/discovery/).
 Note: Currently, discovery is implemented for lights, relays, and simple sensor entities.

shortDesc: use the device as an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy, including active BLE connections
content:
OpenBeken can act as an [ESPHome Bluetooth proxy](https://esphome.io/components/bluetooth_proxy.html) for Home Assistant: the ESPHomeAPI driver serves the native ESPHome API on port 6053 and forwards Bluetooth LE advertisements to HA. On **RTL87X0C** `btproxy` builds it also supports **active connections**: HA can connect to BLE devices through the proxy, discover their services and read, write and subscribe to notifications (e.g. to control BLE locks).

**Setup**
1. Flash a `btproxy` build for your chip (BK7238, BK7231N_ALT, LN882H, RTL87X0C; the BT proxy is always on for RTL8720D/RTL8721DA).
2. Set the startup command (Config -> Change Startup Command), for example:
`backlog BTInit; BTSetScanMode 1; startDriver ESPHomeAPI; BTStartScan`
3. In Home Assistant: Settings -> Devices & services -> Add integration -> ESPHome, enter the device IP and port 6053 (no encryption key). The proxy then shows up as a Bluetooth scanner and BLE integrations use it automatically.

**Notes**
- `BTSetScanMode 1` (active scanning) requests scan responses. Some devices only put important data there, e.g. Tuya BLE devices advertise their protocol version only in the scan response, so integrations for them need active scanning.
- Only one API client (Home Assistant) can be connected at a time.
- Active connections (RTL87X0C): up to 2 simultaneous BLE links. HA writes the notification descriptors itself (the proxy announces the REMOTE_CACHING feature).
- `BTProxyLeds [redChannel] [blueChannel]` drives two LED channels as status lights: blue = Home Assistant connected, red blinking = connecting/discovering, red solid = a BLE device is connected.
- Diagnostics: `BTProxyStatus` logs scan/link state, `BTProxyConnect [MAC] [addrType]` / `BTProxyDisconnect` test connections without HA, and `loglevel 7` adds GATT traces.

Example device: [Tuya Bluetooth SigMesh Gateway JM-MESH01-WG](https://openbekeniot.github.io/webapp/devicesList.html) (CR3L / RTL87X0C), used with a Gimdow A1 Pro Max lock via Home Assistant's `gimdow_ble` integration.
